newsitem.title: GERMANY: Respite for residents in flood-hit eastern Germany.
newsitem.headline: Respite for residents in flood-hit eastern Germany.

text.p: Residents in flood-threatened areas of eastern Germany breathed a sigh of relief on Monday after dikes resisted the pressure of the swollen Oder river overnight.
But thousands remained braced for evacuation at a moment's notice, and officials cautioned against complacency.
"The situation is in no way stable and the dangers aren't over by a long way," said Manfred Stolpe, the premier of Brandenburg, the German state worst hit by the floods.
"We can happily say no further catastrophe occurred during the night. That meant we were able to concentrate on the weak points (in the dikes) which have posed a particular danger."
A fresh wave of high water was expected to roll down the Oder, which forms part of Germany's border with Poland, in the course of the day towards the fertile Oderbruch basin.

"The main task at the moment is to build up defences and to deploy all forces to prevent the worst happening," Stolpe told German Radio. Thousands of soldiers have already been deployed in the country's biggest postwar relief operation.

Some of central Europe's worst floods this century have claimed over 100 lives in Poland and the Czech Republic this month. Germany has escaped the worst of the crisis, but damage to homes and crops has been extensive.

Nearly 5,000 people were evacuated from the most endangered area near the village of Hohenwutzen at the north end of the Oderbruch basin on Friday, and 9,000 were "sitting on their suitcases" in some 24 villages targeted for evacuation.
The region's total population is around 19,000.

"Under this strain the dikes are like pudding," a spokesman for the Brandenburg interior ministry said. "We cannot predict whether the dike will hold. We can only keep hoping and carry Around 700 German soldiers and rescue workers kept vigil throughout the night, reinforcing the dike as a new flood wave that sent water levels to record highs in Frankfurt an der Oder and Slubice in neighbouring Poland approached Hohenwutzen.
Floods were now receding in Frankfurt and Slubice, officials said, but the crest of the wave was expected to pass Hohenwutzen by midday on Monday.
"The next few hours will be the toughest test so far," an official on the flood crisis committee said.
"The water is still far above what's been ever been measured historically," Stolpe said.

"We'll have to be prepared over the next 10 to 12 days for the fact that the dams have weakened and are endangered in many places and that catastrophes could still take place, above all in the Oderbruch region."
Floods in Frankfurt Oder peaked at 6.57 metres (21.54 feet) on Sunday, well above a 1930 record level of 6.35 metres (20.82 feet).
Seven years after unification, officials say flood damage could destroy many east Germans financially, just as they are starting to get on their feet.

The worst damage threatens the Oderbruch plateau north of Frankfurt an der Oder -- a vast plain some 50 km (30 miles) long and 17 km (11 miles) wide that was created 250 years ago by Frederick the Great, who drained the moors and redirected the flow of the river Oder to create the fertile basin for farmland.

Because the area is considerably lower than the river itself, any serious break in the 70 km (45 mile) section of dike protecting the Oderbruch would flood the entire region in a matter of hours, submerging some 17 villages and ruining crops.
Large sections of the dike have collapsed over the past few days, and a 30 km (19 mile) section between Kienitz in the south and Hohenwutzen is particularly threatened.

The highest water levels in Oderbruch were registered in 1940, when measuring stations in Hohensaaten, near Hohenwutzen, reported 7.78 metres, (25.51 Feet) compared to 6.94 now. In Kienitz water levels were at 6.10 metres, near the 1940 level of 6.30.
Further south, there have been three breaks in the dike over the past few days, flooding towns.
The worst hit areas in Germany were Brieskow-Finkenheerd, Wiesenau and Ziltendorf, where the Oder overflowed its banks, rising to the tops of houses in villages some five km (three miles) away.
